openingProblem.problem: In 1958 Khrushchev demanded that the West leave Berlin. In 1961, instead of war, a wall went up across the city, and Western leaders were privately relieved. How did the most dangerous crisis in Europe end with a wall instead of a war?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: who gained most from the Berlin Wall?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Why Berlin again? The ultimatum of 1958
chunks.body:
Ten years after the blockade, Berlin was again at the centre of the Cold War. On 10 November 1958 Nikita Khrushchev demanded that the United States, Britain and France withdraw their forces from West Berlin; soon afterwards he gave them six months to do so. The West treated this as an ultimatum, and a three-year crisis began.

Why did Khrushchev act? The first reason was the **exodus**. West Berlin lay deep inside East Germany, and movement between the sectors of the city was still free. East Germans who wanted to leave could simply cross into West Berlin and fly to West Germany. The flow drained the GDR of workers and showed the world that people were voting with their feet against Communism. The divided city also highlighted the contrast between the two systems: the US held up prosperous West Berlin as a symbol of capitalist success.

The second reason was **West Germany's strength**. Khrushchev wanted to check the growing military power of the Federal Republic, and Judt argues that he hoped to use Berlin as a lever. If the Western powers left and Berlin became a "free city", American credibility in Europe would be damaged and neutralist, anti-nuclear feeling in West Germany would grow. If they stayed, the Soviet Union might trade its consent for a Western promise never to give Bonn nuclear weapons.

The timing reflected Soviet confidence. After the launch of Sputnik in 1957 Khrushchev boasted of Soviet technological superiority and growing stockpiles of intercontinental missiles. Unlike in 1948, West Berlin could no longer be supplied by air: it was too large and too prosperous. Any new blockade would force a far more dangerous confrontation.

The Western powers refused to leave. They argued that the Soviet Union had itself broken the Potsdam agreements by making East Berlin part of the East German state. Eisenhower believed that the freedom of West Berlin required a continuing American presence.

This mattered because Khrushchev's real problem, the flight of East Germans, could not be solved by pressure on the West, which meant that if the West stood firm, the Soviets would have to find another solution.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The exodus of East Germans was the underlying cause.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Khrushchev also had wider aims over West Germany.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Khrushchev wanted to weaken West Germany and US credibility.
Soviet confidence after Sputnik encouraged pressure.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Soviet missile strength was less than Khrushchev claimed.

chunks.title: Diplomacy and deadlock, 1959–1961
chunks.body:
The crisis simmered for nearly three years. Foreign ministers met in Geneva in the summer of 1959 without agreement. Khrushchev and Eisenhower made some progress at Camp David later that year, and a summit was planned for Paris in May 1960. But on 1 May 1960 the Soviets shot down an American U-2 spy plane, and the Paris summit collapsed. Khrushchev decided to wait for the next American president.

Khrushchev repeated his demands in 1960 and again in June 1961, at a summit in Vienna with the new president, **John F. Kennedy**. The threat was always the same: if the Western powers did not leave, the Soviet Union would sign a separate peace treaty with the GDR, hand over its rights in Berlin, and leave the West to negotiate access with an East German state it did not recognise. At Vienna Khrushchev threatened to "liquidate" Western rights in Berlin if there was no settlement by the end of the year.

Kennedy's response combined toughness with restraint. In public he took a hard line: he activated 150,000 reservists and increased defence spending, preparing for a possible conflict. In private, Judt shows, the Americans were more accommodating. Unlike the West Germans, they accepted the reality of an East German state. Eisenhower had told the British Prime Minister in March 1960 that the West could not "stand on a dime for the next fifty years". At Vienna Kennedy assured Khrushchev that the US did not wish to deprive the Soviet Union of its ties in Eastern Europe, a veiled acknowledgement that what the Soviets held, they could keep.

When East Germany began restricting travel, Kennedy publicly reaffirmed the Western commitment to **West** Berlin. By stressing the western half, he implicitly conceded that East Berlin lay in the Soviet sphere. Meanwhile the exodus became a flood: 30,415 people left for the West in July 1961, and 21,828 more in the first week of August, half of them under 25. At this rate, Judt writes, the GDR "would soon be empty".

This mattered because each side made clear what it would not give up (West Berlin for the US, East Berlin for the USSR), which meant that a solution that left both halves in place became possible.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Camp David showed progress was possible.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: His hard line raised the risk of war.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The accelerating exodus forced the Soviets to act.

chunks.title: The Wall, August–October 1961
chunks.body:
Khrushchev cut the knot. On 6 August 1961 the Allied foreign ministers, meeting in Paris, rejected yet another Soviet note. Moscow then authorised the East Germans to close the border. On the morning of **13 August 1961**, on the orders of the East German leader Walter Ulbricht, Berliners woke to find that a barbed-wire fence had gone up overnight between East and West Berlin. Within days it was being replaced by concrete walls and guard towers. Doors and windows of buildings on the border were blocked and then bricked up, and streets and squares were cut in half.

The **Berlin Wall** had three purposes: to stop the flow of migrants, to cut East Germany off from Western influence and to stabilise the GDR. It divided families overnight. The United States quickly condemned it, but did nothing to remove it, because it lay inside the Soviet sector.

The most dangerous moment came in October 1961. A dispute arose over whether East German guards, rather than Soviet ones, could inspect the papers of American diplomats crossing into East Berlin. For the Americans, accepting East German control would mean recognising the GDR. The US stationed tanks at the checkpoint, and the Soviets brought up their own tanks on the other side. For three days, Judt writes, Soviet and American tanks faced each other across the line. A wrong move could have led to war between two nuclear powers. Kennedy used back channels to suggest that if Khrushchev withdrew his tanks, the US would do the same. The standoff ended peacefully, and the Soviets reluctantly accepted the Allied right of access.

The Wall would stand for 28 years, until 9 November 1989, the most famous image of the Cold War in Europe.

This mattered because the Wall solved Khrushchev's problem without forcing the West to retreat, which meant that both sides could accept it, however much they condemned it in public.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It was a confession that the GDR could not keep its people by consent.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Both sides used it to test rights, not to start a war.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Wall became the symbol of Cold War division.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: In practice it reduced the danger over Berlin.

chunks.title: Outcome: a wall instead of a war
chunks.body:
Who won the Berlin crisis? In public, the Wall was a propaganda disaster for the Soviet bloc: a Communist state had to imprison its own people. But in private, Judt shows, many Western leaders were "secretly relieved". For three years Berlin had threatened to become the flashpoint of an international war. Kennedy and other Western leaders agreed that a wall was "a far better outcome than a war"; few could imagine asking their soldiers to "die for Berlin". Kennedy's Secretary of State, Dean Rusk, observed that the Wall "would make a Berlin settlement easier".

Judt argues that the crisis revealed how much the two superpowers had in common. Moscow stopped raising the question of the Allies' status in Berlin; Washington accepted the reality of the East German government there and resisted West German pressure for nuclear weapons. Both had grown tired of their German clients. In the first decade of the Cold War, Adenauer in Bonn and Ulbricht in East Berlin had used their patrons' fear of losing credibility to "blackmail them into 'hanging tough'". Now both superpowers chose stability.

The Germans felt the change. The East German Communists were reassured that Moscow would not sell them out, though disappointed that Khrushchev stopped pressing for a peace treaty. West Germans, seeing the Americans acquiesce in the Wall, grew anxious that they might be abandoned, which is why Washington later repeated its promises, culminating in Kennedy's "Ich bin ein Berliner" speech of June 1963. By then the US had 250,000 troops in Europe.

The Wall ended Berlin's career as the crisis zone of world affairs, Judt concludes, although it took ten years to reach formal agreement on access. Yet the lessons of 1948 had been learned so well that during the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 Kennedy's advisers suspected that Khrushchev's real objective was still Berlin.

This mattered because the Wall stabilised the division of Europe for a generation, which meant that after 1961 the most dangerous confrontations of the Cold War moved away from Europe.

The Wall really ended the crisis.
The Wall was built on 13 August 1961.
The Wall ended the Cold War.

drills.prompt: Question: “‘The building of the Berlin Wall was a defeat for the Soviet Union.’ Discuss.” Which conclusion weighs rather than recaps?

options.text: Judged by propaganda, the Wall was a Soviet defeat; judged by Khrushchev's practical problem, the exodus, it was a success, and since both superpowers preferred it to war, stability rather than victory was the real outcome.
options.explanation: Correct: two criteria and a judgement.

options.text: In conclusion, the Wall was built and stayed until 1989.
In conclusion, walls are bad.
In conclusion, the USSR lost.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent was the emigration of East Germans the main cause of the Berlin crisis of 1958–1961?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.judgement: Whether emigration outweighed Soviet aims over West Germany

modelPlan.thesis: Emigration was the main cause, because it threatened the GDR's survival; but Khrushchev also used Berlin to try to weaken American credibility and stop West Germany obtaining nuclear weapons.
modelPlan.counter: Judt calls Khrushchev's 'free city' aim 'ostensible', suggesting his wider aims mattered more to him.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: What did the Wall solve? The exodus, which suggests it was the problem that had to be solved.

segments.text: The emigration of East Germans was the main cause of the Berlin crisis.
Free movement through Berlin had produced a mass exodus, and in July 1961 alone 30,415 people left for the West.
This meant that the GDR was losing its workforce, so Khrushchev had to close the Berlin escape route, by forcing the West out or, failing that, by building a wall.
However, Judt argues that Khrushchev also hoped to dent American credibility and stop West Germany obtaining nuclear weapons.
Emigration was therefore the main cause, since the Wall, which solved it, also ended the crisis.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “The building of the Berlin Wall was a defeat for the Soviet Union.” Discuss with reference to the period 1958 to 1961.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: By what criterion: propaganda, or Soviet aims?

modelPlan.thesis: The Wall was a propaganda defeat, admitting that the GDR could not keep its people, but a practical success: it stopped the exodus and stabilised the GDR without war, which is why the West was privately relieved.

arguments.claim: For: Khrushchev failed to drive the West out.
For: the Wall exposed the GDR's weakness.
Against: the exodus stopped and the GDR was stabilised.
Against: Western leaders were privately relieved.

modelPlan.counter: West German anxiety after 1961 suggests the West also lost something.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: By propaganda, a defeat; by Khrushchev's practical problem, a success.

segments.text: The Wall was a propaganda defeat for the Soviet Union but a practical success.
Khrushchev failed to drive the West out of West Berlin, but the barbed wire of 13 August 1961 stopped an exodus that had reached 30,415 in July.
This meant that the GDR survived, and the East German Communists were reassured that Moscow would not abandon them.
However, a Communist state had to imprison its own people, which, in public, was a humiliation for the Soviet bloc.
The claim is therefore valid only in propaganda terms; in practice, as Judt shows, both sides preferred the Wall to war.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the causes and consequences of the building of the Berlin Wall in 1961.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which cause mattered most, and which consequence was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: The Wall was built because the flood of emigrants threatened to empty the GDR and diplomacy had failed; its main consequence was to end Berlin's role as the flashpoint of the Cold War.

arguments.claim: Cause: the failure of Vienna and Kennedy's signal.

modelPlan.counter: The Wall also deepened West German fears of abandonment, a consequence that troubled the alliance.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence lasted longest? The stabilisation of divided Berlin, until 1989.

segments.text: The Wall was built mainly because the flood of emigrants threatened to empty the GDR.
In July 1961 30,415 people left, and in the first week of August 21,828 more, half under 25, while at Vienna diplomacy had failed.
This meant that the GDR could not survive with an open border, so on 13 August barbed wire went up, soon replaced by concrete.
However, the Wall also brought a dangerous standoff of tanks in October 1961 before both sides withdrew.
Its most significant consequence was therefore to end Berlin's role as the crisis zone, as Judt argues.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate Kennedy's handling of the Berlin crisis in 1961.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: By what criterion: avoiding war, or defending freedom?

modelPlan.thesis: Kennedy handled the crisis effectively by combining public firmness with private signals of what he would accept, which avoided war; but the price was a divided city and trapped East Germans.

arguments.claim: Signals: West Berlin only; Vienna assurances.
Cost: the Wall and West German anxiety.

modelPlan.counter: His firmness at Vienna may have increased the risk of war and accelerated the exodus.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: By the criterion of avoiding war, Kennedy succeeded; by the criterion of freedom for East Germans, he did not try.

segments.text: Kennedy handled the Berlin crisis effectively, judged by the aim of avoiding war.
He activated 150,000 reservists, yet reaffirmed only West Berlin and told Khrushchev at Vienna he did not wish to deprive the USSR of its ties in Eastern Europe.
This meant that Khrushchev could close the border in the East without a war, and in October Kennedy used back channels to end the tank standoff.
However, the price was a divided city and trapped East Germans, and West Germans feared they might be abandoned.
Kennedy's handling was therefore successful in avoiding war, though it accepted division.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the aims of Khrushchev and Kennedy in the Berlin crisis of 1961.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The aims of Khrushchev and Kennedy

modelPlan.thesis: Both wanted to avoid war and to protect their own side's position, but Khrushchev wanted to stop the exodus and push the West out, while Kennedy wanted to keep West Berlin without challenging the East, so their aims could be reconciled by a wall.

arguments.claim: Similarity: both wanted to avoid war.
Similarity: both protected their own half.
Difference: Khrushchev wanted the West out.
Difference: Kennedy wanted only West Berlin secured.

modelPlan.counter: Both had to manage German clients pressing them to 'hang tough'.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most? It turned out to be smaller than it looked: each could keep its half.

segments.text: Khrushchev and Kennedy both wanted to avoid war over Berlin, but their stated aims were opposed.
At Vienna Khrushchev threatened to 'liquidate' Western rights, whereas Kennedy, while activating 150,000 reservists, reaffirmed the commitment only to West Berlin.
This meant that Khrushchev's real need, stopping the exodus, could be met in the East without touching Kennedy's real need, West Berlin.
However, both faced German clients, Adenauer and Ulbricht, who pressed them to stand firm.
The decisive point was therefore that their real aims were compatible, which is why the crisis ended with a wall.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the reasons why the Berlin crisis of 1958–1961 did not lead to war.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: The crisis did not lead to war because both superpowers preferred a divided city to a fight: Kennedy signalled he would defend only West Berlin, Khrushchev solved the exodus with a wall, and back channels defused the October standoff.
modelPlan.counter: The October standoff shows that war could still have come by accident.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which reason mattered most? The compatibility of the two sides' real interests.

segments.text: The Berlin crisis did not lead to war mainly because both superpowers preferred a divided city to a fight.
Kennedy reaffirmed only West Berlin, and Judt shows that Western leaders were 'secretly relieved' at the Wall.
This meant that Khrushchev could close the border in the East without challenging the West, so neither side's vital interest was threatened.
However, the October tank standoff shows that war could have come by accident, and was avoided only through Kennedy's back channel.
War was therefore avoided because the two sides' real interests were compatible, and careful crisis management kept it so.
